content:
Fireflies.ai meeting transcript

Title: BrightMetrics x Redwood Inference — Cost drivers by route + exports deep dive
Date: Tue, Feb 11, 2026
Time: 10:00 AM - 10:52 AM PT
Duration: 52 minutes

Attendees
- Markus Klein (Redwood)
- Logan Wright (Redwood)
- Nadia Rahman (Redwood)
- Erin Shaw (BrightMetrics)
- Sanjay Rao (BrightMetrics)
- Mina Khatri (BrightMetrics)
- Jordan Lee (BrightMetrics)

Summary (auto-generated)
BrightMetrics asked for a technical walkthrough of Redwood’s upcoming “usage insights” views that attribute cost and latency to developer-defined routes and to model variants. The group discussed route definition (SDK-provided vs gateway-derived), normalization and cardinality limits, and how cost attribution behaves during smart routing/model fallback. BrightMetrics emphasized finance workflows: exports (CSV + JSON), audit logging, RBAC boundaries, and expectations around reconciling console totals with invoice totals.

Topics
- Route tagging options and recommended naming conventions
- Cardinality control and “Unknown route” behavior
- Model fallback attribution: requested vs served model
- Cost metrics in UI and exports: input/output/cached tokens, unit cost, GPU time proxy
- Export job constraints: limits, pagination, retention, audit logging
- Invoice reconciliation and data freshness / late-arriving metering

Action items (captured)
- Markus (Redwood): Send export schema draft (CSV + JSON) and current guardrails (max rows/time window) by Thu Feb 13.
- Nadia (Redwood): Confirm event fields for fallback attribution (requested_model, served_model, fallback_reason) and whether they’re in initial export; share by Fri Feb 14.
- Logan (Redwood): Share route naming/cardinality guidance and normalization rules (length/allowed chars, hashing/rollup behavior) by Fri Feb 14.
- Erin (BrightMetrics): Provide a sample of their route names + mapping to services/endpoints; include any dynamic segments they’re worried about by Fri Feb 14.
- Jordan (BrightMetrics): List required audit log fields and any internal policy requirements for export/download events by Fri Feb 14.

Questions (auto-generated)
- If Redwood falls back to a different model mid-request, does the cost show under the original route and which model does it attribute to?
- Can we export route-level spend weekly and pipe it into our FinOps tooling?
- How do you prevent route tags from exploding cardinality (e.g., user IDs in routes)?
- Are export actions audit-logged and can we scope exports to project-only RBAC?
- Will console totals match invoice totals exactly?

Transcript

[00:00] Markus Klein: Alright, cool. I think we’re all here. Thanks everyone for making time. This is the technical deep dive on route cost drivers and the export/reporting piece. I’ve got Logan and Nadia from our telemetry side. Erin, Sanjay, Mina, Jordan, thanks for joining.

[00:18] Erin Shaw: Yeah thanks Markus. We’ve been waiting for the route thing. Our leadership keeps asking “what endpoint is burning money” and right now we’re kind of… guessing.

[00:28] Mina Khatri: And from finance side, we need something exportable. The console is nice but it doesn’t plug into our weekly close process.

[00:36] Markus Klein: Yep, exactly what this is aimed at. Logan, do you want to set context, like what we mean by “route”?

[00:44] Logan Wright: Sure. So in Redwood, “route” is basically a developer-defined identifier that you attach to requests so we can group cost and latency by your logical endpoints. Think “/v1/chat/support-assistant” or “summarize-ticket” or “product_search.rerank”.

[01:03] Logan Wright: We support two sources: (1) SDK-provided route, like a parameter or header you set, and (2) gateway-derived route if you’re proxying through our gateway and you want it to infer from the request path. In practice we recommend you explicitly set it in the SDK because gateways and reverse proxies can blur the path.

[01:23] Sanjay Rao: When you say “gateway-derived,” does it pick up like the actual URL path or…? Because we have internal routing like /api/orgs/:orgId/assistant.

[01:33] Logan Wright: Right, that’s where normalization matters. If we derived it from raw URLs with orgId, that would explode cardinality. So the plan is: we either take your provided stable route string or, if it’s gateway-derived, we normalize and strip things that look dynamic, and we have hard limits.

[01:52] Jordan Lee: Limits meaning what? Like you’ll reject the request?

[01:55] Logan Wright: Not reject the request. We won’t break inference. But we may coerce route to something like “unknown” or “other” or hashed buckets depending on policy. Nadia can talk about the guardrails.

[02:08] Nadia Rahman: Yeah. Big goal is protect the telemetry system and the customer experience. So we enforce a length limit, allowed characters, and we budget distinct routes per org/project per time window. When you go beyond budget, we roll up into a catch-all. We’ll also surface it in the UI like “Top routes includes ‘Unknown route’” to prompt fixing tagging.

[02:31] Mina Khatri: Ok. We actually see that in other tools, like “unknown service” or whatever.

[02:36] Erin Shaw: Our main question is: if we tag route at our service boundary, do we get cost by route AND by model?

[02:44] Markus Klein: That’s the idea. Route list page: rank routes by spend, show trend line. Click into a route: show model breakdown, latency p50/p95, error rate, and a “what changed vs last week” delta.

[03:00] Sanjay Rao: On model breakdown, one nuance for us: we do fallback. Like we try a cheaper model first then upgrade if response quality is bad, or if it errors.

[03:10] Nadia Rahman: When you say upgrade, is that in your app logic or via our routing policy?

[03:14] Sanjay Rao: Today it’s in our app. We call OpenAI for some stuff, and for Redwood we’d like to do it via your routing eventually, but we need attribution to be clean.

[03:26] Logan Wright: Yep. So our system has two separate concepts: the “requested model” (what you asked for) and the “served model” (what actually ran). If there’s a smart routing fallback—capacity, region, or policy—it can serve a compatible variant.

[03:43] Erin Shaw: This is the big one. If you fall back from say Llama-whatever to something else, does the route cost show up under the original route or does it get split?

[03:53] Logan Wright: It stays under the original route. Route is a property of the request context, not the model. Then within that route, the cost is attributed to the served model.

[04:04] Mina Khatri: So in export we’d see route=“support_assistant”, served_model=“X”, cost=… and maybe requested_model=“Y”?

[04:13] Nadia Rahman: That’s the direction. We’re finalizing exact export columns, but we agree it needs both to answer “why did spend shift?” because if your config is pinned to Model A but we served Model B due to fallback, you want that transparency.

[04:31] Jordan Lee: And do you include a reason? Like “capacity” or “policy” or “region failover”?

[04:38] Logan Wright: In the event stream, yes. In the initial UI we may just show “fallback occurred” at some aggregate level; reason codes might be phase two. But we’ve heard this a bunch.

[04:52] Markus Klein: I’ll note that as a requirement for you all. We can share our current thinking after this.

[05:00] Erin Shaw: Ok. Now, from FinOps standpoint: Mina wants weekly exports. We don’t need perfect real time, but we need it to be consistent and we need to trust it.

[05:11] Mina Khatri: Yeah, and ideally programmatic. Like CSV download is fine short term, but we want JSON too.

[05:18] Markus Klein: The feature includes exports in CSV and JSON. The UI will let you choose time range and filters (environment, region, deployment mode, org/project) and then generate an export job.

[05:31] Sanjay Rao: Export job meaning async? Because some of our queries are huge.

[05:35] Nadia Rahman: Exactly. Async job. We queue it, generate file, then you download. That also gives us a place to log audit events and enforce limits.

[05:45] Jordan Lee: Audit events is my area. What gets logged?

[05:49] Markus Klein: At minimum: who requested export, when, org/project, filters, time window, file format, and then who downloaded and when.

[06:02] Jordan Lee: Is that like in your audit log product, or is it just internal?

[06:06] Logan Wright: It’s in the same audit log feed you already have for console actions. We treat export as sensitive because it’s basically a bulk data exfil path.

[06:16] Jordan Lee: Good. And RBAC? Like can a project admin export only that project?

[06:22] Logan Wright: Yes. The job is scoped. If you don’t have access, you can’t create it, and you can’t download someone else’s export. We also include project ID and actor ID in the audit record.

[06:36] Mina Khatri: We’d also like to attach the export to incident reviews. Like “why did cost spike on route X this week?”

[06:44] Nadia Rahman: That’s why the export includes “compare to prior period” in UI. In export, we’re debating if we include deltas as separate columns or if it’s a separate endpoint. But you can compute it since you have time buckets.

[06:58] Sanjay Rao: Speaking of time buckets, are you storing this hourly or daily?

[07:03] Nadia Rahman: Both. The “top drivers” view is typically hourly for recent time ranges and daily for longer time ranges. We’ll cap how far back you can export at the high resolution.

[07:15] Erin Shaw: What’s the freshness? Like how delayed is the cost data?

[07:20] Logan Wright: It’s near-real-time but not “streaming immediate.” There’s pipeline lag. Also some token metering events can arrive late. So we try to balance freshness vs accuracy. You might see last 15 minutes shifting slightly.

[07:37] Mina Khatri: Does that mean the console won’t match the invoice?

[07:41] Markus Klein: It should match directionally but not necessarily to the penny at any instant. Over a billing period it should reconcile within expected tolerance. There are known mismatch reasons like late-arriving events, cached token accounting, or adjustments.

[07:56] Jordan Lee: Cached tokens? Can you clarify.

[08:00] Nadia Rahman: Sure. If we use prefix caching or KV caching, some tokens aren’t actually computed on GPU. So you’ll see “cached tokens” as a metric. Depending on plan, cached tokens may be billed differently or at reduced effective cost. We want that visible so you can see why a route’s unit cost changed.

[08:20] Sanjay Rao: That’s helpful. Our current vendor just gives total tokens, which is not enough.

[08:26] Erin Shaw: But you said “GPU time proxy” earlier. Is that real GPU time?

[08:31] Logan Wright: Not always. On some deployments we can estimate it based on kernel timing and batch characteristics. We may report it as a proxy. We’re careful about naming because it’s not a literal “billable GPU second” for every case.

[08:48] Mina Khatri: In export, do we get cost per request? Or only aggregates?

[08:53] Nadia Rahman: Aggregates. Per-route/per-model over time windows. Per-request logs are more like tracing and are not part of this initial export.

[09:03] Sanjay Rao: That’s fine.

[09:05] Erin Shaw: Another question: Our “routes” are not HTTP routes exactly. We have internal job types. Like “email_draft.v2” and “email_draft.v3”. Can we do that?

[09:15] Logan Wright: Absolutely. It’s just a string. We encourage stable names and versioning like that is good, because you can see rollouts.

[09:26] Markus Klein: This is actually a pattern we see: use route as the business capability, not the raw HTTP endpoint.

[09:32] Mina Khatri: But you mentioned cardinality budgets. If we have email_draft.<tenant> by accident, does that break things?

[09:40] Nadia Rahman: It won’t break inference, but it will cause rollup. You’ll see a big “Unknown route” bucket, and we may drop the high-cardinality values. We’ll also provide docs that say “don’t include user IDs, tenant IDs, UUIDs.”

[09:55] Sanjay Rao: That’s the thing. We have a gateway that might include org ID in the path, so we need to ensure we’re not relying on the gateway derived route.

[10:05] Logan Wright: Right. If you set the route explicitly in SDK, you sidestep that. If you can’t, then we can help with normalization patterns.

[10:16] Jordan Lee: How do you store route values? Any risk of it leaking PII? Like if somebody puts an email in there.

[10:23] Nadia Rahman: We treat route as customer-provided metadata. We don’t want PII there. We’ll document it, and we enforce allowed characters and length, but we can’t perfectly detect PII. That’s why we have guardrails and guidance.

[10:40] Erin Shaw: Understood.

[10:42] Markus Klein: Maybe we should talk about your exact export needs. Mina, what do you need in the CSV?

[10:49] Mina Khatri: Columns wise: route, date bucket, model, total cost, input tokens, output tokens, cached tokens, unit cost. And we need filters: environment (prod vs staging), region, and ideally deployment mode because we might go dedicated.

[11:08] Markus Klein: Great.

[11:09] Mina Khatri: And JSON: basically same, because our pipeline ingests JSON. CSV is for humans.

[11:16] Sanjay Rao: Also we’d like to understand the model fallback. Maybe have columns like requested_model, served_model. If you don’t have it, we can live, but it would help.

[11:28] Logan Wright: Makes sense.

[11:30] Erin Shaw: And we want “what changed” metrics. Like week over week delta in cost per route.

[11:38] Nadia Rahman: UI will show it. Export might be “two time windows” or “one time window plus previous period” depending on contract. But likely easiest is export both weeks and do diff.

[11:51] Mina Khatri: That’s fine.

[11:53] Jordan Lee: For audit log, we want: actor email, actor role, IP address if you capture it, project ID, filters, and whether the export included any PII fields. Though it shouldn’t.

[12:10] Logan Wright: Actor email yes. IP address we can capture from the console session, generally. We’ll confirm exactly what’s in the event.

[12:20] Markus Klein: We can share the audit event schema we’re implementing.

[12:24] Erin Shaw: On limits: what’s the maximum range? Because if we want monthly exports…

[12:30] Nadia Rahman: We’re still tuning. But we will have guardrails: max rows and max time range for hourly resolution, and then daily rollups for longer. Otherwise people will export billions of rows and it times out.

[12:46] Sanjay Rao: Yeah that’s fair. We got burned with that on Datadog.

[12:50] Markus Klein: Right.

[12:51] Mina Khatri: We can accept daily rollup for long time ranges. Weekly is usually fine.

[12:58] Erin Shaw: Another nuance: We have multiple projects. Like we run prod in two orgs for separate business units. We need RBAC boundaries because people shouldn’t see the other BU.

[13:10] Logan Wright: That’s supported. Everything in insights is scoped to org and project. If you have two projects, you can filter by one, and exports respect that.

[13:21] Jordan Lee: And if someone tries to tamper with query parameters?

[13:24] Logan Wright: Server-side enforcement. We do not rely on client for filtering.

[13:31] Sanjay Rao: Can we talk about latency metrics? Is it per route and per model too?

[13:36] Nadia Rahman: Yes. We store latency p50/p95 and error rate by route and model. For long time ranges, we aggregate.

[13:47] Erin Shaw: Because sometimes we accept higher cost if it reduces p95.

[13:51] Markus Klein: Totally.

[13:53] Sanjay Rao: Ok. Model fallback again: If we do a single request that uses tool calling, could it switch models mid-stream? Like half of it is on one model and then the rest is another?

[14:05] Logan Wright: In Redwood’s routing, typically one request maps to one model execution. But there are edge cases with retries or fallbacks where an initial attempt fails and a retry runs on a different model. In that case, cost attribution should capture the final served model and we also track attempt counts.

[14:23] Nadia Rahman: To be clear, cost is based on what actually ran. So if attempt 1 fails after some tokens, that cost is real. The route’s total cost includes that. Model breakdown would include both models if that happened.

[14:38] Mina Khatri: That’s important. Because in incident reviews, we want to know if a spike was from retries.

[14:44] Erin Shaw: Exactly.

[14:46] Sanjay Rao: Would that look like “error rate up” plus cost up.

[14:50] Logan Wright: Yes.

[14:52] Markus Klein: This is where the “what changed” view is useful. You can see errors, latency, and spend moving together.

[15:00] Erin Shaw: Cool.

[15:02] Jordan Lee: One more security question: retention. If we export, how long is the export file available? And does it respect data residency?

[15:12] Markus Klein: Export files are temporary; we’ll have a retention window for the job artifacts. On residency, files are generated in-region where the data lives. We can confirm exact behavior, but that’s the design.

[15:26] Jordan Lee: We’ll need that in writing.

[15:28] Markus Klein: Yep.

[15:30] Mina Khatri: On scheduled exports: do you support that? Like send to S3 weekly.

[15:36] Markus Klein: Not in the initial release. What we have is manual export via console and an export-job API. Some customers build a small script to call the API and download.

[15:48] Mina Khatri: Ok, as long as there’s an API.

[15:51] Nadia Rahman: There will be an API for creating the export job and then retrieving it. We’ll still enforce rate limits.

[15:58] Sanjay Rao: Rate limits on exports or on insights queries?

[16:02] Logan Wright: Both. Insights endpoints have query cost budgets, and export has its own queue limits.

[16:09] Erin Shaw: Makes sense.

[16:11] Markus Klein: Can we dig into your route naming? Erin, what do you think the top 10 routes are?

[16:18] Erin Shaw: Off the top of my head: “support_reply_draft”, “ticket_summarize”, “kb_search”, “kb_rerank”, “sentiment_classify”, “pii_redact”. And then we have “agent_assist_live”.

[16:33] Sanjay Rao: Plus “chat_internal_ops”. That one is expensive.

[16:37] Mina Khatri: The expensive one is always internal ops.

[16:40] (crosstalk)

[16:41] Markus Klein: (laughs) always.

[16:44] Logan Wright: Those are good. They’re stable and not dynamic. That’ll play well.

[16:50] Sanjay Rao: For env, we want “prod”, “staging”, maybe “dev”. We don’t want someone creating route tags with dev branch names.

[16:59] Nadia Rahman: Totally. We also have cardinality budgets for environment dimension. But generally env is controlled because it’s a fixed set.

[17:10] Jordan Lee: On “route”, can users set arbitrary strings? Like any developer can set it and accidentally leak data.

[17:17] Logan Wright: It’s set by your code, so yes. We recommend you create a small internal helper that maps endpoints to route names and prevents injecting user data.

[17:29] Erin Shaw: We can do that.

[17:31] Mina Khatri: On invoice mismatch, what’s the biggest mismatch reason you see?

[17:37] Nadia Rahman: Usually timing. The console insights are near real time and reflect pipeline ingestion. Invoice is computed from authoritative metering with some late adjustments. Also “cached tokens” can confuse people because they see tokens but cost doesn’t move the same.

[17:55] Sanjay Rao: So in export, do you include like “billed tokens” or “metered tokens”?

[18:00] Nadia Rahman: We include input/output/cached and total cost. The invoice uses total cost as the source of truth. Tokens are there as drivers.

[18:11] Erin Shaw: Ok.

[18:13] Markus Klein: Do you have internal chargeback? Like route spend per team.

[18:18] Mina Khatri: Yes. We assign cost to product teams by service, and route is the cleanest mapping.

[18:25] Markus Klein: Great.

[18:27] Sanjay Rao: Can you filter by “deployment mode”? Because we might have hosted API now, dedicated later.

[18:33] Logan Wright: Yes, filter includes deployment mode.

[18:38] Erin Shaw: Another question: Can we restrict route values? Like whitelist.

[18:44] Logan Wright: Not in product today. But you can enforce in your code. We’ll provide naming best practices.

[18:52] Jordan Lee: We can handle that.

[18:54] Markus Klein: Okay. Anything else on the fallback? That seemed like the big point.

[19:00] Sanjay Rao: Yeah, I want a concrete example. Say I request “redwood/fast-7b” and your system routes to “redwood/fast-7b-q4” or to “redwood/balanced-13b” due to load. In the route detail screen, do I see a bar chart split by served model.

[19:18] Nadia Rahman: Yes, it would show “fast-7b-q4” or “balanced-13b” as separate lines/items. The request stays under the same route.

[19:28] Sanjay Rao: And the requested model is visible where.

[19:31] Logan Wright: That’s the part still being finalized. We have it in the raw events. We can expose it in export first even if the UI doesn’t show it immediately.

[19:44] Mina Khatri: Export-first is fine.

[19:46] Erin Shaw: Yeah.

[19:48] Jordan Lee: If you export requested_model, does that increase data sensitivity? I don’t think so.

[19:53] Logan Wright: Not really. It’s configuration, not user data.

[19:58] Markus Klein: Great.

[20:01] Erin Shaw: Ok. One more thing: we use AWS Bedrock for some workloads. We’re comparing. Their cost allocation is… not great. We want to see per route unit cost and then decide whether to move it.

[20:15] Markus Klein: Understood. That’s a common theme.

[20:18] Sanjay Rao: Also we’ve evaluated Together and Fireworks. They’re quick but the cost reporting is like “good luck.”

[20:26] Markus Klein: Yep.

[20:27] Nadia Rahman: One note: when you compare providers, make sure you’re comparing apples to apples on caching. Some providers hide caching.

[20:36] Mina Khatri: That’s a great point.

[20:39] Erin Shaw: Alright, can we talk about how we set route in the SDK? We mostly use Python.

[20:45] Markus Klein: We can share code snippets. But high level, you’ll pass a route parameter or header. We’re standardizing across Python/TS/Go so it’s consistent.

[20:57] Sanjay Rao: Please don’t make it break streaming.

[20:59] Logan Wright: It won’t. It’s metadata.

[21:03] Erin Shaw: Cool.

[21:05] (brief silence)

[21:07] Markus Klein: I think we’re at the point where next steps are mostly us sending you the schema and docs, and you sending route names and audit requirements. Anything else?

[21:19] Mina Khatri: Can you confirm if the export has pagination? Like if it’s too large.

[21:24] Nadia Rahman: Export is bounded. For very large sets, we’ll force you to narrow time range or filter. The job will fail with a clear error if it exceeds limits.

[21:37] Mina Khatri: Good.

[21:39] Jordan Lee: And the error is audited too?

[21:42] Logan Wright: Export request events are audited regardless of success.

[21:48] Jordan Lee: Great.

[21:50] Erin Shaw: On UI, can we filter route list by prefix? We have “kb_*”.

[21:57] Markus Klein: Yes, we have search. But we’ll confirm exact behavior.

[22:02] Erin Shaw: Great.

[22:04] Markus Klein: Alright. Let’s recap action items so we don’t lose them.

[22:08] Markus Klein: One, we’ll send export schema draft for CSV/JSON and limits. Two, Nadia will confirm fallback fields (requested vs served model, reason) and how it shows up. Three, Logan will send route naming rules and normalization behavior. Erin will send sample route names and any dynamic patterns. Jordan will send audit log field requirements.

[22:33] Erin Shaw: Sounds right.

[22:35] Mina Khatri: Yep.

[22:36] Jordan Lee: Yes.

[22:38] Sanjay Rao: Works.

[22:40] Markus Klein: Great. I’ll send a follow-up email with the list and schedule a shorter follow-up for next week.

[22:47] Erin Shaw: Thanks all.

[22:49] Markus Klein: Thanks everyone.

[End of transcript]
